py-easy-01.rationale: You likely thought int() rounds a negative float down, toward negative infinity, like floor. But int() truncates toward zero, dropping the fraction, so -3.9 becomes -3. Only the // operator floors toward negative infinity.
You may have thought int() leaves the value unchanged or doesn't act on a float. But int() always returns an integer, discarding the fractional part, so -3.9 becomes -3, not the float -3.9.
You may have believed int() only accepts ints or strings and rejects floats. In fact int() accepts a float and truncates it toward zero, so int(-3.9) quietly gives -3 and no TypeError is raised.

py-easy-02.rationale: You likely assumed any value equals itself, so two identical-looking NaN expressions must match. Under IEEE 754, which Python follows, NaN compares unequal to everything, even another NaN. Use math.isnan(x) to test for it.

You may have thought comparing 'not a number' values is invalid and raises an error. float('nan') is a legitimate float, and == simply returns a bool. IEEE 754 makes that result False, with no exception raised.
You may have thought comparing undefined values yields None, like 'no result'. The == operator on floats always returns a bool. For NaN, IEEE 754 rules make the comparison return False, not None.
